messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Since surviving a sudden, life-threatening illness eighteen months ago, Kwame Mensah, a 68-year-old widowed policy analyst, has lived as if the emergency never truly ended. He had been at his desk in a government office building, reviewing a budget brief, when a crushing wave of pain and dizziness came over him so fast that he could not make sense of what his body was doing. He remembered gripping the edge of the conference table, hearing chairs scrape back, and seeing a coworker’s mouth moving before the room blurred. In the ambulance and later in the hospital, what stayed with him was the terror of being trapped inside a body that seemed to turn against him without warning. Even after he was told he had survived, that moment never settled into something finished. Parts of it returned with a peculiar numbness, as if he were describing a stranger on a stretcher, but at other times the memory came with such force that he felt he was back under fluorescent hospital lights, overwhelmed and unable to keep thinking about it.

In the weeks after discharge, Kwame had come to believe that the illness had exposed something irreversible about him. What frightened him most was not only that he might die, but that his own body could no longer be counted on. He was certain now that his body was unreliable, an enemy capable of sounding an alarm at any moment, and he found himself watching it closely for signs of another collapse. That belief kept him tense through the day and night. He noticed every flutter in his chest, every spell of lightheadedness, every shift in his breathing, and even at home in his apartment he felt on guard, as if safety could be revoked without notice. He used to think of home as the one place where he could exhale after work; now he sat upright in the living room listening to his body, unable to settle.

His work as a policy analyst became one of the main places where this threat state showed itself. The ordinary setting of conference rooms, computer screens, and long stretches of concentrated reading had also been the setting of his medical crisis, and sitting through staff meetings could abruptly pull him back into the original moment. A colleague leaning across the table, the stale office air, or the pressure of trying to focus on a dense document could make the memory feel present rather than past. When that happened, his body tightened immediately, his attention narrowed, and he struggled to follow what was being discussed. Sometimes he would stare at the page and realize he had absorbed none of it because he was braced for danger again. The memory itself drove the sense of current threat; once it broke through, he was no longer a man in a meeting but someone in immediate peril.

Over time, the process also ran in the other direction. Because he stayed so alert to his body and surroundings, even minor internal sensations could cue the memory before he fully knew what was happening. A rush of tension in his chest while working at his desk, or the simple awareness that he was alone at home in the evening, could make the hospital scene surge back in fragments. He might first notice that he was suddenly rigid and scanning for danger, and only then find himself flooded with the image of the ambulance doors or the helpless certainty that something catastrophic was happening inside him again. On other occasions he could begin recalling the event in a flat, detached way, only for the emotion to slam into him so strongly that he had to stop and leave the thought unfinished.

As these episodes repeated, Kwame drew darker conclusions about what they meant. Each time his body leapt into alarm in a safe room, he took it as proof that something fundamental had been damaged. He had come to believe he would never feel normal emotions again, because his responses no longer seemed to match ordinary life; either he felt shut down and distant from what had happened, or he was overwhelmed by it. The constant tension and inability to concentrate seemed to confirm his view that his body was still reacting as if danger were ongoing and that he had no real control over it. That interpretation made him more watchful still, especially at home, and more convinced that another medical disaster could arrive without warning.

By the time he sought help, the strain had narrowed his life considerably. He still went to work, but tasks that once suited his careful, analytic mind now took much longer, and he had begun quietly declining some meetings because he feared freezing or losing focus in front of colleagues. Evenings in his apartment were the hardest; without distractions, he felt his body on alert and waited for it to betray him again. What finally brought him in was the sense that he was no longer living after the illness but remaining inside it. He said he wanted, more than anything, to feel that the event was over, but he was afraid that if he could not trust his own body, he would never again be able to feel safe, or fully himself.
